opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's been faster than I expected, and I say that as someone who was working on it directly. If you'd asked me a couple of years ago, I think I would have said IMO gold was plausible eventually, but I wouldn't have bet on it happening as soon as it did, and certainly not with a general-purpose reasoning model writing natural-language proofs rather than a specialized system working in a formal language.

What surprised me most wasn't just hitting the score threshold. It was the kind of capability it reflected. Olympiad problems aren't about recalling a technique. You have to sit with an unfamiliar problem for hours, try things that don't work, notice small structural clues, and then build a careful argument that holds up to a skeptical grader. Seeing a model sustain that kind of extended, creative reasoning was a real qualitative shift, not just another point on a benchmark curve.

And what's happened since has, if anything, reinforced that feeling. The same underlying ideas around scaling reasoning and test-time compute have been carrying over into harder and more open-ended settings: research-level math, tricky coding problems, scientific reasoning where there isn't a clean answer key. A competition problem has a known solution that someone already found. The more interesting frontier is whether these systems can help with problems nobody has solved yet, and we're starting to see early, real signs of that.

So my honest calibration lesson has been that I tend to underestimate how quickly things move once the right general methods are in place. I try to hold my predictions more loosely now. There's still a lot that's hard: reliability, knowing when you're wrong, really long-horizon research. But the trajectory has consistently come in ahead of what I would have guessed.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's been faster than I expected, and I say that as someone who was fairly optimistic going in. If you had asked me in early 2024 when a general-purpose model, not a specialized system with formal verification bolted on, would get gold at the IMO, I probably would have said several years out. Instead we had a model doing it in natural language, under the same time constraints as the students, within about a year and a half.

The thing that surprised me most wasn't the raw capability, it was how it arrived. There was a period where the common view was that you'd need something like Lean, a formal proof checker, to make progress on hard math, because otherwise how do you know the proof is right? And that approach did make real progress. But what ended up working was more about getting models to reason for a long time, to be honest about where their argument has gaps, and to self-correct. Those are much more general skills than competition math. That's why I think the IMO result mattered beyond the headline. It was evidence that scaling up test-time reasoning transfers to problems that take hours, not minutes.

Where my expectations were wrong in the other direction is on what comes after. I think a lot of us assumed that once you clear IMO gold, research-level math is just around the corner. It's closer than it was, and we're seeing models contribute to real open problems, help with lemmas, find counterexamples. But there's a gap between solving a problem that a human wrote with a known answer and deciding what's worth working on in the first place. That taste part, the part where a mathematician spends months on something because they sense it's important, that's still mostly human. So the pace on benchmarks has been faster than I thought, and the pace on genuine autonomy has been more like what I expected, which is to say steady but with real friction.

astra-6.text:
It’s been faster than I expected. Olympiad mathematics is challenging because you need more than knowledge or the ability to carry out calculations—you have to find an idea, build an argument around it, and make sure that argument actually works. I expected getting to gold-medal level to take longer.

But I also think it’s important to distinguish that milestone from what comes after it. An olympiad problem is designed to be solvable, and you know there’s a relatively short solution. In research, you may not know whether the question you’re asking is even the right one. So reaching gold-medal level is exciting, but I wouldn’t treat it as automatically solving the problem of doing mathematics. What makes me optimistic is the pace at which these systems are getting better at reasoning through difficult problems.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s been faster than I expected. A few years ago, I thought getting to IMO gold would require a much longer period of steady progress. Instead, we’ve seen models go from struggling with these problems to producing really sophisticated proofs in a surprisingly short time.

But I’d distinguish doing well on the IMO from doing mathematical research. The IMO gives you a well-posed problem, and you know there’s an elegant solution. In research, choosing the right question and figuring out which directions are worth pursuing are a huge part of the work. So reaching gold is an exciting milestone, but what I’m most curious about now is how those capabilities translate into discovering new mathematics.
